pos.text:
I picked up Octopath Traveler expecting “another JRPG,” and it ended up being one of those games I kept thinking about even when I wasn’t playing.

The HD-2D art style is gorgeous. Like, I stopped multiple times just to look at towns at night, the lighting, the water, all that. The music is also insanely good — it makes even random exploring feel important.

Gameplay-wise, the combat is the main reason I stayed. The whole Break/Boost system feels really satisfying, and it stays fun because you’re constantly planning turns instead of just spamming attacks. Each character having a “job vibe” and different tools keeps fights from getting stale (most of the time).

Story is… mixed, but in a way I still enjoyed. I like the idea of 8 separate stories, and some of them are genuinely great. But it can also feel a bit disconnected, and the “party” doesn’t always feel like a real group since

I played a demo of this game years ago on another system, and I thought it was generic. Years later, I bought it on a Steam sale(because I love Square Enix), and shoveled it into the backlog. Today, I am playing it, and I can't believe I thought it was generic. When I play this, I get the same sense of adventure that I did when I used to role-play Dungeons & Dragons. There is something about it that sparks my imagination. I am glad that I gave it another try. And, what is fun to think about... when I am finished with this game there is a second one already available with a third one on the way. Sometimes, things just happen like that... Sort of like how my whole life I never listened to Motorhead or KISS until a year and a half ago. Now, I have all of these albums to discover.

I thought this game was stupid when it first came out. Many years later and I find myself very much enjoying it on Steam Deck. Safe to say, this game is an awesome intro to JRPGs. Sometimes games just don't find you at the right time. Glad I gave it a second chance.

A diamond in the rough. Octopath Traveler screams classic SquareSoft/Enix JRPG homage. And it is in many ways. The presentation and art direction are just eye-candy, the soundtrack (from Yasunori Nishiki) and the combat leans to a more simplistic side but it's still engaging and challenging without relying on cheap tricks. It escapes being merely nostalgia bait to something that stands on its own. It isn't for everyone though, and can only be recommended for people who truly enjoy turn-based RPGs or have prior experience with JRPGs in general.

PROS:
*Insanely eye-catching and visually beautiful visuals and effects that blend in perfectly with the retro pixel 2D style.
*Path Action system brings a new layer of interactivity with NPCs rather than them being just textboxes.
*Non-linear structure from the very start adds a great replayability factor.
*Boost and Break system from Bravely Def

It's good.  Pretty grindy.  Some of the stories are better than others.  I have completed all the character chapters and unlocked all the special jobs.  I don't have it in me to grind out the optional "final" boss.  I have almost a million Octopath-bucks so can purchase whatever gear I need, I simply don't have the will to grind out a bunch of levels on dudes I don't enjoy playing just so I can beat the true ending.

You're not going to figure everything out unless you have LOADS of time or use internet searches to find out what you need.  I dig this, but also don't dig this.  It involves you in the world when you actually have to pay attention in order to figure out quests, that's more cool that it isn't cool...but then sometimes I just want four of a particular accessory to make a boss easier, so I Google where to find them since i have no desire to talk to every NPC and open every c
Lots of fun short stories that ties together nicely for some unexpected world-building towards the end. I love JRPGS and I'm looking forward to trying the next one.

Quite a fun game. Art, music, story and characters are all quite good. The gameplay is great and the Break and BP systems are very fun and feel great to use. While it's no Press Turn it is still quite a step above most Turn-Based RPGs.

The exploration was great. It does the pseudo-open world thing that Unicorn Overlord does where you can reach later areas with the risk of higher level enemies for the reward of better gear, shops and higher exp enemies. The areas all look great as well.

Random encounters still really suck. Doing it purposely as a throwback to old rpgs where it also sucked, still makes it suck now. The only way to reduce the encounters is to start/recruit 1 of the specific characters or find a shrine for the job which you'll only be able to do mid-game.

Fleeing is also awful. It starts at what feels like a 30% chance and is only reliable once 3 Flee attempts fail. Even

Started, stopped, and then restarted the game after nearly 100%'ng Adventures of Elliot. Generally enjoy most of the characters, the combat feels rewarding, and stealing items from every NPC is wonderful.

Probably won't 100% the game but will be seeking out all endings and will then move on to OT2. 

Grab the demo if you haven't tried. Play Elliot if you haven't played that as well.

TLDR: buy on deep discount and go in with low expectations. If you're not hooked by the core gameplay loop after playing one or two chapters, the rest isn't going to do it for you. 

I picked up this game on sale wanting a fairly chill, old school RPG experience on the Steam Deck (on which it runs brilliantly).

The premise of the game is that you can experience 8 different character paths, so I started with the dancer, Primrose (who has one of, if not the best, story in the game). Right out of the gate, the story grabbed me - tragedy, loss, mature themes, questions about purpose and identity. 

Combat felt dynamic and satisfying - your goal is to experiment by attacking each enemy with different types of attacks to determine their weakness, then "breaking" their shields to stun them. The job system was compelling and addictive. The music is top tier. Visually it's an absolute treat. The

I spent 107 hours with the game, completing most of the content and reaching the true ending (and to say that it wasn't easy is to say nothing, you have to do a LOT to reach true ending). The reason I was hooked was the satisfying gameplay loop. I enjoyed the combat and music; it's simply a joy to play, despite the fact that the theoretically core gameplay is weak. Most of the story (Alfyn, Primrose, Othilia, Tressa, Haanit) is a boring snoozefest, and the dialogue in this game is terrible, looking like it was written by a 5-year-old.

So, most of the stories sucks, but the game was redeemed by other elements.

I bought this with my Christmas steam gift card and got to say it was extremely attention grabbing and sucked me in til 1am which is late for me being first shift. Great pixel art and music. I enjoyed figuring the battle system. Very solid game at 9/10.

July 5th 2026 update: I completed this game with 170 hours. Game was worth every penny. The Secret Final boss was an absolute pain but that's part of the challenge. Figuring out the combos of the classes in battle was fun. Primrose was my favorite character and I found Tressa the best Character in the game.

It's good but not great.

The graphics are impressive for a pixel-art game, gorgeous even. That's really all I have to say about that, we all know graphics don't make or break a game.

The music is really good, but not great. I found myself humming and whistling a few of the tunes while not playing the game. But the bar for music in Square RPG's has been set so high that I can't call it great -- it's not Final Fantasy tier.

The combat can be fun, but it can also get old. It kept me engaged enough to keep coming back to the game, but I was usually getting sick of it by the end of a session. The battle is pretty strategic for a turn-based JRPG -- mindlessly attacking or just casting your strongest spells is not the way to go here. Enemies have weaknesses to certain weapons or elements, and you'll want to plan your actions accordingly to maximize damage and disrupt their turns.

This game was fantastic it is honestly one of the best turn based rpgs I have played but one down side is that in late game it does get a little grindy trying to level up the characters.

Beautiful game with a genuinely charming cast and a combat system that keeps you engaged, but the random encounter rate will test your patience in ways the actual bosses never do. Still worth it, just be prepared to fight the same three enemies approximately ten thousand times before you finish.

After spending over 100 hours with Octopath Traveler, I have mixed feelings — but mostly positive ones.

The music is outstanding and never gets old, even after such a long playtime. The HD-2D visuals are beautiful, and each character’s story is emotional and memorable.

However, the gameplay started to feel suffocating over time. The combat system is fun at first, but grinding and replaying content for all achievements became exhausting. Trying to 100% the game almost made me sick of it.

Still, despite the fatigue, it’s a great game with a strong story and amazing atmosphere — just better enjoyed at your own pace.

The game itself is great!  The combat is fun, the graphics are gorgeous, I feel everything is really well-designed.

I don't care at all about the story though.  They made it so artificially slow-paced that it's a struggle.  In cut scenes, a common theme is to watch your character s l o w l y walk over, stand in place for 5 seconds, then watch a little icon pop up over their head.  Then another character might do it.  Then they might begin the process of thinking about preparing to consider the possibility of talking.  When they do eventually talk, it's so dull and cryptic.  I really, really tried to get interested in the story, but every cut-scene is like that, and due to the technique, about two paragraphs of dialog feels like it takes ninety times longer than it'd take to read if they just went with a style that didn't try to artificially force drama at you.

But again, the combat

*Play this game before octopath traveler 2, the QOL features in octopath traveler 2 can make this game unenjoyable for some*
Probably my favorite series for classic cozy rpg, octopath traveler is a game you take your time with. Characters are well written, the graphics are some of the coolest I have ever seen, and the battle mechanics are refreshing enough to keep the battles from getting stale. I also like the fact that the game feels very open world, you can tackle the stories at your own pace and have plenty of resources so you do not feel pressure to stick to certain areas, along with the ability to flee if above ones ability to defeat the enemy. This is an HD-2D style game as well, having modern lighting effects and many cool visual elements that would not have been possible in the past. It adds a very interesting feeling to the game, as through you are playing something old and new

Octopath Traveler is an absolute masterpiece. Its stunning HD-2D pixel art is some of the best in any modern RPG, and the turn-based combat is endlessly fun, strategic, and satisfying. Each of the eight characters is lovable in their own way, with personal stories that are engaging and full of heart.

From visuals to gameplay to character charm, everything comes together beautifully.

Verdict: ★★★★★ (5/5) – A must-play for anyone who loves JRPGs, artful storytelling, or pure RPG nostalgia done right.

Octopath Traveler review

Preface
When Octopath Traveler came out in 2018 it felt like a breath of fresh air. JRPGs have come a long way since the 90s. But that's not necessarily always a good thing. While more complex stories, more cinematic experiences, and more action elements can be enticing. The nostalgic simplicity of well-designed turn-based combat seemed to have been largely tossed to the wayside during the 7th console generation. This game is exactly what I wanted and needed in 2018. However, there were flaws with the game back then, as well as more I have found retrospectively. 

The good
It would be wrong to begin this section with anything but the music. Yasunori Nishiki did an unfathomably good job directing the music. So much emotion is conveyed that it's honestly unreal. Conviction, depression, wonder, relaxation, and everything in between. No tutorials are needed for comb

I liked this game.  Loved the art style and the music and the surprisingly mature stories for each traveler. I was expecting their stories to all come together much more than actually happens.

This title will really try your patience with the lack of direction.  I have plenty of time to spend playing video games but come on, the way side quests work just wastes your time for no good reason.  Have fun talking to every single NPC on every map.  Collection achievements but no in game tracking?  You can't even tell if you've been in a dungeon already or not.   Having the true ending be an extremely difficult secret super boss behind an eight miniboss gauntlet with no save point wastes your time for no good reason.  What's that?  You thought you could use your team setup you've grown accustomed to during the entire game?  LOL, no, you have to go back and grind your B team up in level and giv

First Pick H'aanit, can't change character, mad.
Capture OP Monster, beating fallen god, stay at hell you ♥♥♥♥♥, madness channeled, not mad anymore.

Good game

Not what I expected, and in a good way.  The battle system for additional effects and damage is really nice, but the story is what absolutely took me.  I really feel like this sort of pixel game does better for the experience than flashy graphics would, and keeps me from getting distracted from gimmick battles that interrupt the flow of the story.  It's a shame this is Squaresoft's oddball rather than the norm now.

Good game even if I was trolled by the secret boss.

Remember you need ALL your party members to be decently leveled before doing the last boss. Got lazy since I lost so much progress.

Main issue is the lack of QOL. Quests/PurpleChests/Scrutinize a lot of small, but really annoying things.

I wanted to go for 100%, but it was just annoying.

Definitely still worth playing despite all that.

An RPG reminiscent of the Final Fantasy series, Octopath Traveler pairs modern graphics with a wonderfully cozy style. While the story doesn’t quite match FF's depth, the engaging combat system, gorgeous art style, and brilliant soundtrack easily make up for it. As someone who deeply values a game's aesthetic, I highly recommend it. An extra bonus: despite its updated visuals, it remains remarkably lightweight, requiring minimal storage and resources.

The only thing I’d change is making it easier to play in the background. Currently, the mouse gets trapped inside the window (even in windowed mode) requiring a press of the Windows key to free it.

this game is very good and i loved every moment.
even characters i thought i wouldn't like, the story for each of them was just amazing.

Octopath Traveler starts with a very ambitious premise. 
We have eight characters and unlike other RPGs where the members of your party can have their own substories but do share the main one, here we're really talking about a story for each of them. These all occurs in the same world and yes, these members do form a party of eight along the way. This "party building" is done rather unnaturally, each member gets added just because of "You look strong" and "I could use an hand" reasons, although it's literally the first time they meet each other. Each character doesn't play a part in other characters stories, they will comment on the situation from time to time with some small event talk but that's it, they only participate in the battles.
Setting this forced party thing aside, the main problem resides more in the quality of the stories. I noticed players having

Absolutely too many random encounters, little to no overarching plot, nothing ties these people together nor do they really interact with each other at all. It's just more disjointed side-stories.

anyone who tells you there is no grinding in this game is lying to you: there are eight total characters. the four who aren't in your party don't get exp from combat. and you cannot remove one of them from your party. so that is at a minimum three different party groups that need to level separately in order to progress through the game.

apart from that the story doesn't make sense narratively. for some of these characters there's no reason for them to party up with others. you walk up to them, they tell you their life story, you kill a boss with them, and then they're just in your party forever. there's not even any dialogue between party characters, the only time they have dialogue is when they're on one of their story missions, and the rest of your party isn't involved.

I really want to like this game, and I did at first, because the visuals are superb. The use of the 2.5D, depth of field, and pixel art combine to make the game beautiful. Furthermore, the OST is fantastic (Battle II is an all timer imo).

What caused me to abandon the game though is its lack of depth. There are thirty two individual chapters divided into four per character, where they all occur in the same manner. Enter a beautiful, but unoriginal, town → talk to people there → encounter a problem → use character action → find out a boss needs to be defeated → go to a dull cave or forest → defeat boss → celebrate → repeat. It relies solely on this formula, making the narrative not only repetitive and predictable but also superficial. I made the mistake of starting with Octopath Traveler II, which is one of the best recent JRPGs. Now, the original one pales in comparison, and since the plots are unrelated, it's very hard to recommend the first Octopath.

From graphics and music to depth and fluidity of the game mechanics, the sequel simply improves on everything. As a result, this game simply feels janky and a chore to play. There's more grinding, less skill options in combat and exploring, worse voice acting, and the default controls are even less logical than in the sequel.

While Octopath traveler is still a servicable turn-based JRPG, the average player misses nothing if they skip this and start with Octopath Traveler II.

I started playing this game after I bought it on sale, I gave it a shot, It didnt pull me in so i decided to come back to it. After picking it up back up I just felt like I should play something else. I also did not get far into the story of the 8 characters. It was just not enough to draw me in. The art style and the quick turn base combat are very good. Its a slower pace game that I just couldnt get invested into it. 
I don't see myself finishing this game.

Graphics are great, combat is fun, characters are cool.

It's a shame everything else is uninteresting and disjointed. If you're bored of epic tales and ensemble casts, check this out. If you like a cohesive and interesting story that's story driven and narrative focused, pass on this.

This game isn't worth the price tag at all. The main story lines are all rather short and easy to beat. After that the late game is comprised of optional quests. I am glad Square is making more turn-based RPGs, but I did not care for Octopath Traveler. The game is extremely grindy and combat is very slow. Having eight main characters sounds fun in theory, but it also means keeping your characters properly equipped and at an appropriate level to progress the story is a tedious slog. Furthermore I did not find any of the protagonists' stories to be particularly interesting. I would rather have one good campaign than eight mediocre campaigns.

this game is just boring. 80% of your playtime is cutscenes because there's 14 main characters. this would be fine if any of the characters or their stories were at all interesting, but they aren't. they're all quippy and low stakes. 

"my character arc is.. finding a lost book!"
"mine is.. travelling around to sell stuff!" 

jesus christ could we get any more humdrum. 
additionally, the balance is hella skewed and all but forces you to grind. you will not be of sufficient level for the next areas just by doing story; you WILL need to sit in an area and run around grinding random FF style encounters. new party members start at lvl 1 ALWAYS, so you are HEAVILY penalized for not bumrushing to all 201739 party members across the world map

Tentative thumbs down.

Is it a good game in general? Certainly. The graphics are great, the story is serviceable, the mechanics scratch a nostgalic itch that will really hit the spot for some.

Is it a good game for me? No. It cemented to me that some things are best left in the past. I thought I was nostalgic for a FF or Chrono Trigger like. Maybe if the story was more adult it could have worked for me. But it was too cutesy in all aspects to go longer than a dozen hours or so, much of which is just traversing empty maps with random mob battles. Beautiful pixel graphics are not enough.
The art style is really nice, but the plot and characters are nothing worth investing in. Which makes every single interaction with the game feel like a grind to me.

This game could be so much more. The environment is so vibrant and beautiful, the music is other-dimensional, and the boss designs are quite unique and a fresh breath of air. 

However... 
the main story leaves  a lot to desire. The eight traveler stories barely overlap in any way, and the plot twists are generic and predictable. I wish there were more side stories that personally involved each of the eight travelers and fleshed out more of their background. Finally, the side quests scattered in the world are not very straight forward to solve. waited 20 hours for it to get good, never happened. dont waste ur time on this. 

stories are all mini arcs bound to the character and don't tie together at all, gameplay is on the level of most rpgmaker games

play the sequels, they're prolly better
Story was awful, gameplay was generally fun.  -1 +1 = 0.  Do not recommend.

I made the mistake of starting with Octopath Traveler II, which is one of the best recent JRPGs. Now, the original one pales in comparison, and since the plots are unrelated, it's very hard to recommend the first Octopath.

From graphics and music to depth and fluidity of the game mechanics, the sequel simply improves on everything. As a result, this game simply feels janky and a chore to play. There's more grinding, less skill options in combat and exploring, worse voice acting, and the default controls are even less logical than in the sequel.

While Octopath traveler is still a servicable turn-based JRPG, the average player misses nothing if they skip this and start with Octopath Traveler II.
